speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hockin that Bill C-12, an Act respecting museums, be read a second time and referred to a Legislative Committee.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Chair is only waiting for the House to calm down before recognizing the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mrs. Gibeau) who had the floor when the House took recess at 1 p.m.

Madam Speaker, I shall continue, by saying that from the moment the original National Museums Act was adopted in 1968 through the implementation in 1972 of the relevant national policy, we had come a long way in recognizing the important role of government in this area.
After 21 years, the Act needed some adjustments to give us the opportunity to better meet today's challenges. As a matter of fact, it is because of the major impact these institutions have on our society that in January 1986 the Richard-Withrow task force was set up to look into our policy in that area. It is therefore after extensive consultations with specialized institutions and interested Government agencies, and after a review of the recommendations by the Standing Committee on Communication, Culture, Citizenship and Multicultural-ism that this bill respecting museums was drafted.
On the one hand this bill provides for a more comprehensive political framework of operation and on the other hand it gives to the four museums under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Government greater autonomy. In line with the task force, recommendations September 1986 the bill grants Crown corporation status to the following institutions: The National Gallery of Canada, which includes the Canadian Museum of Contemporary Photography; the Canadian Museum of Civilization, which includes the Canadian War Museum; the
May 25, 1989

Canadian Museum of Nature; and the National Museum of Science and Technology, which includes the National Aviation Museum.
Granting Crown corporation status to our museums will increase their administrative flexibility, while taking into account the individual history of each of these institutions and the specific nature of their collections.
In keeping with recommendations made by the study group and the Standing Committee on Communications, Culture, Citizenship and Multiculturalism, the legislation provides that each of these museums is to be a Crown corporation; this confirms their public responsibility with respect to cultural matters and gives them operating independence to reach full development. Each organization will thus be able to assert its museographic and museologic role more forcefully. They will also seek different objectives which reflect their individual character.
Madam Speaker, this new legislation aimed at creating museums which will be better prepared to serve Canadians establishes the following organization structure.
First, a hierarchic framework which defines the responsibilities of each decision-making level. To that extent, each museum assumes its responsibilities but comes under a board of directors which reports to the Minister responsible to Parliament.
Second, the appointment of active board members who will establish a credible link between the hierarchic framework of responsibility of each organization and of the Government.
Finally, the board of directors of each museum is empowered to set a course of action which is consistent with its specificity, with reference to the over-all Gov-emement cultural policy. This course of action will be in accordance with the rules and procedures of a cultural
Museums
agency, but the Government will not interfere with its daily operations.
The new act also provides that they will not restrict their activities to the National capital area. They will be encouraged to develop their program of travelling exhibitions, artefact loans and professional service exchanges with the overall museum community. This will become a vital aspect in assessing their yearly corporate plan.
This structural change is significant, because the four new Crown corporations will be subject to part 10 of the Financial administration Act, while until now they were subject to the same financial requirements as Government departments. However, in order to respect the principle of administrative autonomy that should prevail in the case of Crown corporations with a cultural mandate, the measure establishes a special relationship between them and the Government, by providing that cultural activities, including the acquisition, maintenance, conservation and use of museum material are not subject to ministerial control. Neither are public-oriented activities and programs such as exhibitions and publications.
Each museum will be responsible for its own staff. Under part three of the Bill, and after consultation with labour unions and orgnizations involved, transitional provisions ensure that staff are transfered from the current system to that of the Canada Labour Code, while remaining subject to the Public Service Superanuation Act.
This measure recognizes and encourages the essential role of the four new Crown corporations in cultural matters. Our intent is to give more emphasis to the social mandate of museums in Canada in the context of the future pointed to by their recent developments, so much so that they play a significant social role in this country and have become a source of pride throughout the community.
Since the inception of a geological commission in Canada, in 1842, which was to lead to the establishment of the National museum of Canada, the erection of the new architecture of the National Gallery of Canada, and

May 25, 1989
Museums
that of the Canadian museum of Civilizations and the National Aviation Museum, a long scientific and technological process has endowed our institutions with rich collections and professionalized the services rendered to the community.
In that respect, they remain the gardians of our heritage and their function is to gather and classify art collections, heritage objects and techniques and scientific specimens. A number are research institutions that help widen our knowledge in various scientific fields. But it is through the dissimulation of that knowledge that museums are essential tools in shaping our Canadian identity. Therefore, through their collections and knowledge, they are also in many respects new places of learning, which puts them among social institutions of the future. Because they are not subject to a specific program, they have the flexibility to reach a number of publics through various modes of communication and learning and also to impact on all age groups in our society.
Since they are appropriate venues for recreation and culture, museums are entertainment centres that can provide a recreational dimension without neglecting their educational role in Canadian society. We know that they can now compete economically with other recreational destinations and focus public attention very effectively. A balance should therefore be sought between expanding their audience and maintaining the fundamental role we described earlier.
Madam Speaker, that is why government and museums must work together to provide a satisfactory framework for collecting, preserving, interpreting and enhancing collections that are representative of our Canadian and world heritage, for the benefit of present and future generations.
By tabling this legislation, we are providing the government and all Canadians with a cultural instrument that is effective, better adapted to present-day reality and better suited to the fundamental role society expects it to play. These museums will therefore be entering a new development phase in which they will be able to pursue their objectives, which are to preserve, to do research, to circulate and to educate, in terms of their specific mission and the responsibility they now have to the public under this legislation.
We are thus discharging our responsibility as defenders of our Canadian heritage and offering Canadian society the necessary tools to become acquainted with its own culture and that of other civilizations. These four new Crown corporations will be much-needed partners
in developing, with the museum community, the cultural policies of the future.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak to Bill C-12, an Act respecting museums. The purpose of this Bill is to dismantle the National Museums of Canada Corporation. May I assure Hon. Members that this decision was not lightly taken.
Under this Bill, the individual responsibilities of each board will be clearly outlined and their mission clearly defined. The effectiveness of the seven national museums' goals will be enhanced in great measure and it will be to everyone's advantage. The changes are designed to allow the national museums to serve all Canadians better. The responsibility, authority and accountability of the directors of the National Gallery of Canada, the National Museum of Science and Technology, the Canadian Museum of Civilization, the Canadian Museum of Nature as well as those three museums which fall under their mandate will be increased.
I believe that Bill C-12 is a living testament to the spirit of parliamentary reform. The process of a task force study followed by the Standing Committee on Communication and Culture's review which acted upon a consensus provided very sound advice to the Government. At this time, I would like to pay tribute to the Parliamentary Secretary who is sitting in the House at this time. He chaired the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture and worked very hard to enable a sense of commitment and consensus to emerge. I believe this allowed for a team response in the interests of the cultural communities of Canada. I take my hat off to the Hon. Member. I only wish that the new Standing Committee will learn from this experience.
As a result, we have before us a Bill that has been thoughtfully prepared. It was arrived at through consultation and consensus building. I hope that it will serve Canada's national museums well, and I trust it will serve as an important example of a solid, valuable process that will continue in this Parliament. From a management perspective, I believe we will be better served. Certainly architecturally, we will be better served. We have been enriched. Our cultural and collective heritage will be better housed, protected and displayed in the magnificent National Gallery in its new glass home, the exciting, expansive and yet to be unveiled Canadian Museum of Civilization, the dynamic mind-expanding Museum of Science and Technology and of Nature, the up and coming Museum of Contemporary Photography as well as the new modem home of National Aviation Museum.
May 25, 1989

The Canadian War Museum has been neglected, and I hope, will be attended to in the near future.
Madam Speaker, a people that is ignorant of its history and heritage cannot, in my humble opinion, fully assume its national identity. Granted, in this century of instant communication, when the day's events, whether they occur in Peking, Moscow or Montreal, are all projected on our television screens often live, we often have the impression that technology has taken the place of memory. However, that is certainly not the case for everyone. As in other areas, there is an increasing tendency to go back to the grass roots of our collective memory. Last year, more than 20 million people visited Canada's 846 museums. Now that is impressive! We think of the National Gallery of Canada, a truly brillant example of our Canadian cultural heritage, and the immense success it has enjoyed since its official opening.
I am sure that the soon to be opened Canadian Museum of Civilization will add a new dimension to our cultural network. Generations of Canadians will be grateful to Prime Minister Trudeau for having the necessary vision and determination to give this country these two masterpieces, the National Gallery of Canada and the Canadian Museum of Civilization.
What also impresses me, however, is the fact that 60 per cent of Canadian museums are quite small and spread out over this vast country of ours. I wanted to mention this aspect, Madam Speaker, because it is essential if we want to ensure that our natural and cultural heritage is accessible to all Canadians and that Canada's regional and cultural diversities are adequately represented.
In the Bill before the House today, we are basically dealing with seven large museums which are the backbone, as it were, of our Canadian museum system. The National Gallery of Canada, the Canadian Museum of Civilization, the Canadian Museum of Nature, the National Museum of Science and Technology, the Canadian Museum of Contemporary Photography, the National Aviation Museum and the Canadian War Museum, as a group, provide a network of information, helping us to
Museums
understand the development of the universe and its inhabitants, from prehistoric times to the space age.
There is no doubt in my mind that in addition to preserving our natural and cultural heritage, museums remain an important link between generations, because they explain the past and project the future of the cultural mosaic that is Canada.

I would like to deal with some background, Madam Speaker. What were the issues that led to this Bill about our National Museums of Canada Corporation? I think it is important to focus on the question. We need to understand how it became a worth-while goal to amalgamate these autonomous museums and through that amalgamation the shared use of administrative and financial services. There is a common thought today that bigger is better rather than small is beautiful. This amalgamation make it possible to pool scarce resources and to avoid duplication. These centralized services were to reduce the burden of housekeeping for the four museums and to provide more cost-efficient services.
Furthermore, to those sponsoring the legislation, the combining of four separate institutions and the three subsidiary ones was thought to be more desirable since the resulting single museum corporation was likely to be more forceful in its dealings with the Government. While on paper it appeared to be a more effective structure, the system in practice was too heavy, inefficient, costly and some would say overly bureaucratized.
While the national museums are similar in that they collect, study and exhibit objects and are owned by the federal Government, that is where the similarities end. The museums actually collect and exhibit very different kinds of museum objects from different kinds of disciplines. These really need to be better focused and their efforts need to be better directed in order to get the best response for all our Canadian citizens. What was originally felt to be in the public's best interest led to much loss of autonomy and conflicting priorities. With

Museums
this ambiguity over lines of authority, the situation basically became unworkable.
In January of 1986 the Government appointed a task force charged with examining the federal policy concerning museums which reported back in September of 1986. The principal recommendation of that task force was the repeal of the National Museums Act of 1968 and the dismantling of the corporation. This was to be followed by new legislation to establish each of the four major federal museums as administratively autonomous, freestanding institutions.
The task force also recommended a restructuring of the museums assistance programs, the principal means of providing grants to museums outside of Ottawa. There is a world outside of this National Capital Region, as we all know.
The assistance programs were to fall under the direct responsibility of the Department of Communications and its Minister and to be administered by an Assistant Deputy Minister upon the advice of an advisory committee.
The Standing Committee of Communications and Culture undertook to review the task force recommendations. A series of most interesting hearings were held during the fall of 1986. Our committee was able, I believe, to hear the varying views from institutions and from individuals that supported many of the task force's recommendations. It enabled us in our January, 1987 report to the House of Commons to be fair and to show consensus along all lines.
On May 21, 1987, the Minister of Communications reported to Parliament that the Government was going to establish these separate national museums, abolish the corporation organization and place the granting programs which serve museums and galleries throughout Canada in the Department of Communications. The task force summed up the corporations' problems well when they wrote, and I quote:
Its centralization of functions, instead of facilitating the implementation of museum programs, the Corporation has enmeshed them in bureaucratic complexity, so that coping with that, is what consumes and exhausts staffs' energy, relegating creative work to a secondary role.
I was pleased that we moved ahead with this action. While for the most part I find that Bill C-12 is a really good piece of legislation, I would like to make some of the following observations. Let us get down to some of the nitty-gritty part of the second reading for which we have a very serious responsibility to this House as fiduciaries of the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Well, to my hon. colleague who writes all those wonderful books about how this House operates and who is really the master of the process in this House, we could have used your enlightened involvement in the debate which just took place recently. Notwithstanding that, I do respect your opinions in this regard. I forgot to mention the Hon. Member is from the riding of Etobicoke-Lakeshore. We shared the equality task force report. That is a landmark report that I would appreciate adhering to all along the way. Disability week is coming up and we will remember that all over again as we roll with Rick Hansen.
Clause 23 provides for the appointment of a director for each museum by the board of the museum subject to the approval of the Governor in Council. I would have preferred to have seen the model used to appoint a director like that of the National Arts Centre. That appointment is made by the board and is not subject to Governor in Council approval.
When appearing before the Standing Committee on its Estimates the other day, the Secretary General of the corporation stated that the model used in Bill C-12 was not their favourite choice. He said: "It would not have been our original first choice. It is a move in the right direction but one could argue whether it goes as far as it should". I would suggest that in the end he was satisfied with the compromise. I still have to ask, is not the power and responsibility of the board diminished in this way? Can we expect them to act as a responsible body if they do not have the ultimate responsibility? Will not a director feel he must serve two masters? Finally, what is to be achieved by making an appointment subject to Cabinet approval?
The museums' relationship with Government is also of concern to me. For museums to function effectively, they must have the necessary autonomy and arm's-length from Government. The best formula is that recommended in the Applebaum-Hebert Report which stated:
May 25, 1989

"Large subjective decisions of an aesthetic, artistic, professional, subventionary nature are best taken collegially by a board of directors acting at arm's length from the Government of the day".
I note in Clause 27(1) that the Government cannot give directives to museums regarding:
(a)	the acquisition, disposal, conservation or use of any museum material relevant to its activities;
(b)	its activities and programs for the public, including exhibitions, displays and publications; and
(c)	research with respect to the matters referred to in paragraphs (a) and (b).
However, in Clause 27(2) there is to be no interference regarding the content of the by-laws of a museum with respect to its cultural activities. The question to be answered when the Bill goes to legislative committee will be: what is a non-cultural matter? I asked the museum corporations and the general public, if they are interested, to perhaps respond to this particular concern, if it is of concern to them.
Bill C-12 should provide no lesser independence from Government for museums than has already been established for the Canada Council, the CBC, Telefilm Canada, and the National Arts Centre.
The variations in the statements concerning objects, capacity, and powers of the four museums is quite interesting. Each museum essentially contributed to its own mission statements. Generally, the powers are similar, except for the Canadian Museum of Nature, which is the old Canadian Museum of Natural Science, and its well enunciated research mandate that one finds.
For example, the Canadian Museum of Nature is empowered to create new knowledge and synthesize existing knowledge into new patterns and models. It is to provide facilities to permit qualified individuals to use and study collections, to foster the co-ordination of collection-based data in Canada, to promote scientific literacy and a better understanding of nature by demonstrating the inter-relationship among all organisms including human beings and their environment. I find that a creative and a new approach. It defines where we are in today's evolving technology, whether related to museu-mology or any other aspect of our living, as was pointed
Museums
out this morning, when we debated the new radio-communications Act.
Through these clauses it would appear that research has been given a more powerful foundation at the Canadian Museum of Nature than at the other museums. With respect to the responsibilities to teach, to train docents, and to give courses, when I asked that question, I was told that Clause 6(l)(e) is found in the mandate of all museums, and is deemed large enough and comprehensive enough for both the museum activity within the museum itself in terms of teaching and training docents as well as it would be for Canada and throughout the world. I hope that the museum community is satisfied with Clause 6(l)(e) which states:
promote knowledge of and disseminate information about works of art and other museum material in its collection and art in general, throughout Canada and internationally-
It does not state in a city or in-house. I hope it is clear enough to give the mandate I know the museums presume they have and certainly need to have. I wish to bring that to the Minister's attention and perhaps it can be discussed.
I raised another issue during a briefing session with the museum people with respect to the Bill. That related to copyright. I am pleased to see many people who were responsible for the writing and the consultations around this Bill are present in the gallery. Welcome, and thank you for the job that you did.
Hear, hear!

Bill C-12, through each of the museum mandates, provides the power: "to destroy or otherwise dispose of works of art and other museum material in its collection". In discussion with them I brought to their attention the problems that could be confronted under the Copyright Act. I raised concerns about the potential conflict with moral rights in this new copyright Bill that is presently in action. The museum officials have assured us, and I quote the Director General: "that museums will be bound by copyright law, and that any action to destroy would have to be governed by the provisions of the copyright law". Any artists who are worried about destruction of their works of art need not be concerned.
Under Bill C-12 the Canadian War Museum is a submuseum, if I may put it that way, although it should be a full museum in the fullest sense of the word, under

May 25, 1989
Museums
the Canadian Museum of Civilization. Concern has been expressed that, by falling under the Canadian Museum of Civilization and not having its own board of directors, it will get lost in the shuffle.
There are also concerns in the military community, particularly among veterans, that the War Museum has been downgraded through its loss to the National Gallery of 6,000 square feet, and an annual acquisitions budget of only $65,000. That is barely enough to keep it alive. This museum has a collection worth more than $500 million. It contains works by a large number of our Canadian Group of Seven artists. Because of a lack of space its holdings are not easily viewed. It is our heritage and contribution to Canada, to Canadians, and to the peace of the world that is hidden away from public view. Much of the collection is rarely seen, but it is worthy of being seen. I hope that something will be done. I also hope the aspiration of the veterans will be met for more recognition for Canada's military history and eventually more exhibition space to display those works of art. It is a worth-while goal and worthy of consideration.
When representatives of the National Museums Corporation appeared before us, I was very interested to hear about the whole question of multiculturalism which we address. I am glad the Minister is present. I hope he will read the transcripts. I think he will be very pleased as his mandate is being performed and outlined as we look at the evolving role of Canadian public policy, as well as the policy of the museums. He said that while the galleries are now very sensitive to aboriginal art and the history of our nations, and while our primary reliance on references in the legislation is to Canadian culture, it encompasses the whole spectrum of multiculturalism as experienced within Canada. I like that answer. The Secretary General went on to say: "I believe there is a strong commitment to exhibiting in a substantive way the multiculturalism richness of this country". We were pleased to have this confirmed through the director of the Canadian Museum of Civilization, Dr. George Macdonald, who outlined rather elaborate plans.
I believe it is important that the multicultural community knows about these plans, so I am pleased that the Member for Saint-Laurent (Mrs. Maheu) received very explicit answers for us to be able to share with the House today as we celebrate our approach to the realization of
the new museums mandates. We are seeing Museums being responsible for showing all the cultures of this country, in all their richness and variety, and in all of their Canadian diversity and dimensions. We were very pleased to read the five-point program outlined by the Museum of Civilization.
The establishment of five different exhibits, ranging from a children's museum to the electronic exhibit, is very exciting. I hope this commitment is not impeded by the Government's attempts to cut back. It is so concerned about the deficit that it forgets that culture is part of life. It cannot cut everything down to the size of a deficit. I hope this commitment will add to our understanding of Canada's evolving multicultural heritage. I quote Mr. Macdonald who explained:
First of all, there is the special exhibit that we will have on the Chinese in Canada as our first focus on a group from outside of Canada who brought a rich cultural heritage. This will open on June 29. We have involved Chinese communities right across the country in this exhibit.
The exhibit belongs to them as well as to us, and can be shared by everyone. He went on to say that they will come to Ottawa or send their representatives from their communities. The museum will also prepare for when the show travels across the country so that those residents in each area will be familiar with the exhibit. They can begin to involve members of their community and interface between their community and the broader community, using the exhibit as a doorway between their cultural heritage and the Canadian culture in general.
I hope this type of activity will be taken up by many other cultural communities who have come here to enrich Canada and provide the foundation that makes up the colourful and glowing tapestry of this country.
We have been producing material for the networks and television programs that are increasingly carried on the cable systems, servicing different language groups across the country. The fact that more than 200 hours of interviews have been filmed with the Chinese community is a very exciting and creative approach which I certainly hope will help increase our community understanding more. They have an equal amount of material on dance in the different ethnic cultures.
May 25, 1989

They are also developing concepts for exhibits in children's museums which will emphasize children reaching out to children. If our children can destroy those stereotypes that are often passed along subconsciously in the environment in which they live, we will live in a healthier Canadian society.
They have also developed the first in what I hope will be a series of films on the civilization of mankind. The first film is entitled "The First Emperor of China". It is a joint production with the National Film Board in the celebration of its fiftieth anniversary. This film has great potential both economically and technologically, and will be sold around the world. We can be very proud of what the museums are accomplishing through their very confident staff.
When we begin using the electronic highways in this creative way, we can cross the world with much greater ease and certainly cross the boundaries of Canada to display our ancestral home as well as our chosen home. This new creative approach is very exciting and dynamic.
I want to deal with the question of acquisitions. Our national museums have very shallow root systems. We have never had the great private collections or fortunes which created European and American museums. We did not get started in the second half of the 19th century when the museum movement hit its stride in those countries.
Objects are now so dear that it is utterly out of the question that we should be able to get sums of money that would get us anything that is worth while. Fortunately, that has not been the case, although we have been very lucky with some donors. It is clear that we have been quite successful in obtaining many valuable collections from some of our Canadian patrons of the art. However, this was with very limited Government resources, resources that unfortunately have not increased in many years.
The Cultural Property Review Act has provided not only our national museums but museums and galleries across the country, through tax benefits, a valuable method of acquiring art. However, massive increases in the value of works of art mean that there exists in this country numerous major works of art whose current market value would trigger tax benefits on gifting far
Museums
greater than the owner can use even with the five year carry forward provision of certification.
While the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is so debt reduction conscious, it would be worth-while for him to give serious consideration to some action to allow a cultural enrichment approach in planning the Budget, and to balance our Canadian collective heritage with that of reducing the public debt. I suggest that our collective memories will stay much longer than the Minister of Finance.
It will be impossible for any public institution to acquire the works of art of this quality that we are missing if we do not do something about making gifts and bequests easier for the owners and Canadians to give to Canada.
I remind the House that it was under the Government's management two years ago that a major painting by Gustav Klint was lost to Canada because no museum could come up with the $2 million required to match the generous offer of the Cultural Property Review Board. This situation could have been avoided. This stingy short-sightedness has deprived our country of a few very valuable pieces of collective remembrance.
There is a concern over the Museum Assistance Program, the Canadian Conservation Institute and the Canadian Heritage Information Network Program. When the plan to dismantle the National Museums Corporation of Canada was announced, the previous Minister announced the devolution of these programs, and they were to fall under the Department of Communications. The Government also discontinued the mu-seumobile program. The $2 million from the museumobile program was to be added to the Museum Assistance Program. This commitment has not been put into effect despite repeated requests from the Canadian museum community.
The program was created in 1972 to help museums and galleries across the country improve their standards so that they may receive better, more interesting exhibits. Money had been used to upgrade exhibit space, humidity and temperature control, security, loading and unloading areas, workshops space, fire prevention systems, supplies and equipment. This program has been of great assistance to Canada's nearly 2,000 museums but unfortunately the $8 million allocation has not increased in 17 years, since 1972. We are all guilty of this neglect.

May 25, 1989
Museums
The Canadian Conservation Institute has ongoing facilities. The Canadian Heritage Information Network, with a little bit of foresight and money, could become a very important financing vehicle as it can self-finance and be sold across the world. The idea of an inventory of all heritage artifacts and artistic objects for all museums is an exciting idea.
I suggest that much is left to be done. There is a very dynamic and exciting project for museums outside the National Capital Region. We have a document that needs to be addressed. I hope that it is put into place shortly. We need to assure all Canadians that we are aware of their existence.
I find it rather ironic as I conclude my remarks that we are addressing the future of our national museums and their collections and yet we have not given the kind of attention to that group which makes much of this possible. I refer to our artists.
The 1981 census data indicates that there are approximately 135,000 professional artists in Canada who are responsible for plays, books, paintings, sets, sculpture, music, film, poetry, cartoons, advertising and images that permeate our daily lives, and that they not only contribute but are part and parcel of our national culture and heritage. Yet this is not reflected in their income levels, in their treatment by Government tax laws and policies, labour laws, working conditions, health and safety regulations, social benefits, business development assistance and so on. Nor has the Government done a great deal to improve their situation with the tax changes. Hopefully, we will do justice soon to this section of our society.
Our national museums are a source of our Canadian heritage, culture and pride, a visitor's delight that enriches all who visit. The mission statements are in place. Secretary General John Edwards of the National Museums Corporation did a fine job in devolving the corporation. He is out of a job and deserves a new one.
Let us hope that with the mission statement in place the mandates will be matched through public fiscal will, joined by private sector generosity, supported by dedicated volunteers, so that their life and purpose will grow and flourish. There is much more to museum life than just structural change.
Hear, hear!

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hockin that Bill C-12, an Act respecting museums, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to follow the speakers from the Government side and the critic for the Liberal Party, my colleague and friend from Mount Royal. She spoke about the rights of the great many artists in our country. I invite her to support my Private Member's Bill which I will be introducing. It deals with the rights of artists. I think she will find it an interesting Bill. I would appreciate her support.
With regard to Bill C-12, I would like to make five points about the legislation. First, the process has been a good one. I want to indicate the nature of that process and say why it has been a good one.
May 25, 1989

Second, I want to say that on behalf of the New Democratic Party, for which I am the culture and communications critic, we support the Bill in principle.
Third, I want to say a few words about the adjustment procedures in the Bill. We want to ensure that all the employees who work for these museums, the hard-working people who keep the museums going, are well treated.
Fourth, I feel compelled to say a few words about the appointments to the various boards since this measure will be adding boards of directors. You know what happens, Madam Speaker, when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) gets his chance to appoint a few people to boards of directors. He just cannot resist all those plums. I want to say a little bit about the plum pudding in this Bill.
Fifth, I want to point out in a positive way a criticism that this is only half a policy, that the Conservatives' long awaited national museums policy is still that-long awaited. It is time for the Government to deliver on an outstanding promise to Canada's museum community. We have not heard from it yet. I want to say something about that.
The process that has developed on this legislation over the past four years has been generally positive and worth while. It is sort of an exemption to the normal rules around here, and perhaps that is a good exemption.
First, we had the Richard Withrow Task Force which recommended in September of 1986 the dismantling of the Museums Corporation. Then, the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, of which the Parliamentary Secretary sitting opposite was an outstanding chairman, supported unanimously the recommendation that four major federal museums be established as autonomous institutions, each with an explicitly stated legislative mandate and its own board of trustees.
I want to note as well the previous Member of Parliament from Broadview-Greenwood, the NDP Member Lynn McDonald, who was the culture critic for our Party and who did a lot of hard work in this area.
The Government gave a generally positive response to the committee recommendations in May of 1987. After consultations with the unions and museums, a Bill has
Museums
been produced which for the most part reflects the work of the last few years. It seems to me that it was a good process.
I said that we would support this Bill. The intent of the Bill is to dissolve the current Department of Communications corporation, the National Museums of Canada, and replace it with four Schedule I Crown corporations. They are the National Gallery of Canada, including the Canadian Museum of Contemporary Photography; the Canadian Museum of Civilization, including the Canadian War Museum; the Canadian Museum of Nature; and the National Museum of Science and Technology, including the National Aviation Museum.
As the task force suggested, and the standing committee agreed, this new arrangement should permit each museum and its own separate board to operate more independently and gain additional control over their own future direction. Under the existing structure, these federal museums all have to spend a much greater share of their resources on administration and other non-programming activities. Under the present arrangement, operating as a departmental Crown corporation, the National Museums Corporation board had some significant limits to its independence. As a Schedule I corporation, these powers will be broadened. Thus it can be a more active board.
In addition, the Government has been expressly forbidden from directing the museums on matters of a cultural nature. In other words, it has built into it an arm's length relationship with regard to Schedule I Crown corporations. That relationship is built in by the nature of its being a Schedule I Crown corporation.
A few years ago the House reformed Crown corporations. We created ones with different schedules which had different mandates and different set-ups. The Government has to keep its fingers away so far as that is possible from the directors running Schedule I corporations. The principle of arm's length has not always been respected by previous Conservative Ministers of Communications. I hope it will be maintained here. Of course, it is up to the museums themselves and their boards to ensure that with their new independence they respect their mandates as institutions respective of and responsive to Canadians. They should not become isolated from Canadians.

May 25, 1989
Museums
This leads to a problem as I see it. It is that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) will now have four boards to appoint members to instead of one. That raises the old problem.
I will give Hon. Members an example of what the old problem is. I have raised it in the House before. I refer to the previous Minister of Communications who is the Minister of Communications again. He was the Minister of Communications before he became the Minister of Energy. He is now Minister of Communications again. I refer to one Oscar Masse, as we call him over here, the great Oscar winner. I would like to look at some of the previous appointments.
I refer to one Denyse Patry, who was the Prime Minister's former secretary at the Iron Ore in Sept lies. She was appointed a director of the Canada Council. Louise Dionne is a dressmaker from Sept lies who worked on the Prime Minister's campaign in Manicoua-gan. She was appointed to the Canada Council. Rodrigue Trembley, who is the last of the Sept lies three, as I call them, was the Prime Minister's riding campaign manager. Where did he end up? The National Museums of Canada Board. Jean Lougheed, the wife of Peter, where did she end up? Canada Council. Thomas Assaly, a noted local Conservative fundraiser and Ottawa developer, where did he end up? On the National Arts Centre Board. When he was appointed to the Board he was furious because he thought he would get his parking paid for, and when he found out he could not, he demanded it. He thought he would get free parking, he thought that was what it was really all about. Finally he tried to make the Centre pay for his own parking tickets.
Then of course there is the famous Jean Sirois. He was the campaign manager of Michel Cote, a previous Member of this House and previous Minister. Mr. Sirois' spending habits were legendary. The other appointment was Pierre Boutin, who is a relative of Jean Sirois and he was also appointed. He became chairman of the-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: A point of order.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: On a point order, the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do appreciate that the Hon. Member is endeavouring to score some debating points and that is one of the ways this House works.
I would just remind him that there is an avenue and a vehicle for examining the qualifications of members of boards-
That is not a point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: -and that he as a Member of the Standing Committee on Communications, Culture, Citizenship and Multiculturalism is at liberty, and has been at liberty to examine the qualifications of many of the individuals to whom he is referring.

It is not a point of order. If the Parliamentary Secretary wants to take part in the debate, he should take part in the debate or have someone else take part in the debate.
The fact is that these were appointments made by the previous minister of culture who is now the minister of culture and communications. They were appointments made to cultural institutions in Canada. He now has the power under this Bill to appoint not one board but four boards of directors. Those previous appointments were not only bad for ethical reasons. They badly hurt the Canadian cultural institutions to whom these people were appointed.
Jean Sirois' tenure at Telefilm was a nightmare of incompetence, political interference and personal overspending. Pierre Boutin oversaw the debacle of the National Arts Centre trying to choose a new director. We had to have a special committee meeting of the communications committee of the House because they were so incompetent it took them two years to choose a chair. The reason they were incompetent was because on the boards they had too many political appointments.
Tory hats.

There were Tory hats on the boards. That is what it was about. When Flora MacDonald became Minister she changed that situation. I gave her credit for that. She started making changes. Now that we have Oscar Masse back, we are into the possibility that we are going to have more Tory hats appointed.
Yesterday, at the communications committee, Pierre Juneau, the President of the CBC testified. He is a very discreet, distinguished man. He was asked by one of my colleagues on the board: "Well, would you make any suggestions now that you are leaving public life after 20
May 25, 1989

or 25 years?" He said it in a sort of nice way. Do you recall? He said: "I say to the Government, not so many political appointments to the board of cultural institutions."
Let's hear about Juneau's appointment.
The Hon. Member yells: "Tell us about Trudeau's appointment."
Juneau's appointment.

Juneau's. Well, it is the same thing, is it not, Juneau, Trudeau? Almost. The fact is that these boards have been hurt by the appointments. I will leave it there. I do not have to belabour this. I made the point. With talented, committed people in charge, these institutions will grow and flourish, which is what we all want in every part of this House.
Now, I want to say a few words about- [Translation]
When it's one of your colleagues who is appointed to the United Nations, like Stephen Lewis, it's OK!

Yes, my colleagues know that. My colleagues from the West too.

I was talking about transitional arrangements because it is important in this Bill. One of the major concerns before us is to ensure that transitional arrangements for the museums are acceptable to the employees who work there. I have consulted with the unions involved and some of the employees who work there, and it seems for the most part that the legislation is acceptable in this regard. There may be a couple of problems-I hope my friend, the critic for the Liberal Party will listen to this because she is going to have to deal with it in committee.
There may be a couple of problems with transitional matters as far as the employees are concerned, but we will have to deal with that in the legislative committee on this Bill and we will have to look at that very carefully. We might want to have witnesses from the employees or the unions.
I know for example that the Professional Institute for the Public Service has contacted me with some concerns
Museums
on these matters. There would be a good witness. In general, it should be noted that the Bill changes the status of labour relations at the museums. At present they are subject to the Public Service Employment Act, or the Public Service Staff Relations Act. Under this Bill, the independent museums will fall under the Canada Labour Code. In general, I see this as a positive step due to the greater number of issues that can be dealt with in collective bargaining under the Canada Labour Code. It is probably positive but we will hear from the unions and employees involved at committee to see whether any changes have to be made there.
Finally, I said that this was only half a job. It should be noted and noted strongly that while we in the NDP support this legislation in principle, it does not mean that we are satisfied with the Government's museum policy.
Indeed, as Mr. John MacAvity of the Canadian Museums Association has correctly noted, it represents only half a job. In response to the standing committee, the Government promised a national museums policy to cover not just the museums here in Ottawa but museums and galleries across the country. That is very important. Every MP will be able to tell you, my colleagues here behind me from areas in British Columbia, in Penticton and up in Prince George, that there are lots of small museums with a lot of people who are interested in them. I know many retired people in some towns who have a lot of time to get involved in museums. They are museums all across the country. The standing committee found, and people in the country feel that there needs to be a national policy to deal with these museums outside of Ottawa. Since the recommendation we have had a government discussion paper Challenges and Choices, and repeated further promises of action.
Museums in the regions cannot just simply survive on these promises. These institutions play a critical role in collecting, preserving, researching and interpreting Canada's cultural heritage. I think successive federal governments, including Liberal governments, have let them down. The Museums Assistance Program was created in the early 1970s. It has not received so much as an increase for inflation since that time, not even a 1 per cent increase in 16 years. It is as if the governments did not believe that inflation counted for museums outside of Ottawa. These museums do not have the magic

May 25, 1989
Museums
formula of avoiding inflation. They need more money. They are' hurting.
The museums' policy has been promised for a long time. I say to the Parliamentary Secretary that we were told back in January that it was drafted and ready. There have been some disturbing signs lately, however. There was no mention, unless I missed something, in the departmental estimates. The museums' policy was missing in the Throne Speech as well.
Last week, on International Museums Day, the Parliamentary Secretary made a statement congratulating the Museums of Canada and especially underlining the contribution made by volunteers to those institutions. I agree with him. It was a good statement. The Government should have celebrated International Museums Day, not only with those words from the Parliamentary Secretary but rather with actions from the Minister of Communications. Those actions would mean a museums policy.
Let me summarize the New Democratic Party's position on this Bill.
First, the process has been good. It follows up a commission and a committee report. That is the way it should be.
Second, the principle of the bill is good, mainly to make these museums four Crown corporations. Schedule 1, Crown corporations, gives them more room, if you like, to be even better museums.
Third, we have to look at the adjustment procedures in a little bit more detail in the legislative committee to make sure the employees are well treated.
Fourth, as I pointed out, it does raise the spectre of those plums that the Government would like to give as political appointments. Instead, the Government should appoint good people. They can have political backgrounds but it is not necessary that they do not have and that should not be the sole criteria. The criteria should be to encompass people who are competent and who can act as advocates for the cultural agency. They should be advocates for their own agency with the Government. That is the secret of having a good cultural board.
Finally, this is only half a policy. The other half will be the long-awaited national museums policy which will apply not just to these wonderful museums in Ottawa but to museums outside the capital.

Madam Speaker, I will be brief because I know there are several colleagues across the way who would like to participate in this most important debate.
I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this legislation because museums are a vital part of our cultural history. They remind us of our past and the steps which our society has taken to make possible the quality and standard of living which we enjoy today.
Our museums remain the guardians of our heritage. They are responsible for assembling and classifying collections of works of art and heritage objects.
Let me thank the Hon. Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), if she is listening, for briefly flagging a matter that I raised two days ago before the Standing Committee on Communications, Cultural, Citizenship and Multiculturalism. The witnesses in front of our committee were the Board of Directors of the National Museums of Canada. I want to enter into the record my profound concern that what is currently known as the Canadian War Museum comes under the broad umbrella of the Canadian Museum of Civilization. I know that displays are not permitted in the House of Commons. I am not going to show all of this poster which advertises the grand opening of the Canadian Museum of Civilization, June 29,1989.1 will quote the slogan at the bottom of the poster which states: "A new experience in museum entertainment".
The Canadian Museum of Civilization is the mother of a sub-museum called the Canadian War Museum and the current Act calls the civilization museum a celebration of human cultural achievements. I believe there are several hundreds of thousands of Canadians who would take a very dim view, indeed, of the description of the victims of World War I and World War II as a celebration of human cultural achievement, let alone a showcase for museum entertainment. I am appealing to this House to remove the Canadian War Museum from under the umbrella of the Canadian Museum of Civilization, because the wonderful Canadian heritage we are talking

about here is the opposite of celebration. It is commemoration in its fullest sense.
Good.
I want to see, by whatever procedural routes that are necessary, and I think I can count on my friends across the way-
Absolutely.

-a fifth museum corporation to honour the memory of the 150,000 men and women who fought and died in the two world wars, the thousands more in the Korean War and the United Nations Emergency Force in the Middle East.
There is no reason in the world, in my view, that the Government cannot establish a Canadian memorial museum. I dislike resurrecting the use of the word war, but I intend to move at the earliest opportunity, in the legislative committee, a statutory amendment to ensure that the Canadian memorial museum be completely autonomous, reflecting the views of those Canadians who lost loved ones from 1914 to 1918, from 1939 to 1945, from 1950 to 1953 and beyond. I believe that they deserve to have their own distinct and separate museum.
The National War Memorial goes a long way toward establishing that but it is not quite the same thing as preserving the heritage and the memorabilia of those Canadians who lost their lives in serving this country.
It was 50 years ago that the King and Queen opened the National War Memorial. What prompts my intervention today is that we are coming up to the fiftieth anniversary of the declaration of World War II. On September 9, 1939, Canada entered World War II. We are talking about a quiet display or a memorial to the men and women who gave their lives, not only in that war but in previous and subsequent horrors and catastrophes around the world.
Can we have a somewhat more autonomous memorial museum portray the colours of sacrifice that our Canadian war dead and other heroes and heroines across this country displayed in the name of this country? It can be done very simply. I conclude by bringing forth this recommendation which we can refer to a legislative committee.
Museums
George C. Bell, the President of the Canadian Institute of Strategic Studies, says we can do it simply by:
In 1988 establish the museum as an autonomous institution with a new name, a clear mandate, its own board of trustees and consultative committees and budget. Couple this with an announcement of an immediate preparation of a development plan for the museum and an appropriate national support programs.
The new name could be the Canadian Military Heritage Museum or the National Military Heritage Museum.
My suggestion would be to set up the Canadian Memorial Museum in honour of all of those wonderful men and women who gave their lives and set up their support for this country. I hope in the course of the next few minutes that we could refer Bill C-12 to the appropriate legislative committee and see if we can get justice done by separating and creating an autonomous committee for the Canadian Memorial Museum out from under the Museum of Civilization.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott). Has he been able to ascertain what the additional costs would be in order to take this important memorabilia, the $500 million worth of paintings and related items, give it proper packaging and proper respect and environment. As well as this project which he is talking about and, is something I do support.

Madam Speaker, in specific dollar terms, no, but I can tell the Hon. Member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Mills) that throughout Canada through the Department of Veterans Affairs there are regional museums, places to put the memorabilia about which we are talking, places where the memorabilia could be collected as part of a national memorial museum for which space could very easily be allocated or reallocated since space was already taken away from it some years ago. I think we could find an appropriate location and appropriate facilities, but right now, the important thing is that the Government signal the importance of the symbolism of this matter and make certain that somehow, somewhere, for Canadians now and in the future, there is a place to remember the Canadian men and women who died in the various wars in which they fought.

May 25, 1989
Museums

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member knows that across Canada there are 700,000 members of the Royal Canadian Legion. What would the Hon. Member think of organizing collectively? Since we all agree on this issue, the forces of this institution, 1 am sure we would get support for this cause?

Madam Speaker, that is a very worth-while question. That is what the legislative committee is all about. That is why legislative committees are set up to follow second reading of an important Bill such as this. With the collective agreement of every single Member of the House of Commons, agreement that I see right now, and with the 700,000 plus men and women of the Canadian Legion, we can get that momentum going and get that institution set up in honour of those who died in our world wars.

Madam Speaker, I hope that I can finish my remarks by the top of the hour. As usual, my colleague from Mount Royal has delineated our Party's position on this issue very well.
I am very pleased to see a piece of legislation that allows Canada's four national museums to evolve into independent bodies. This is a step forward and is great progress for these fine institutions. The legislation is based upon the recommendations of the Richard-Withrow task force on federal museums policy which set out a coherent policy for Canadian museums.
The four new national museums, the National Gallery, the Museum of Civilization, the Museum of Nature and the Museum of Science and Technology, will be independent arm's length cultural institutions in the tradition of the National Arts Centre, the Canada Council and the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. The museum will join these institutions as important components of the Canadian cultural mosaic.
In the tradition of Canada's arm's length cultural institutions, we must ensure that the museums are completely autonomous in all matters relating to their collections and activities. I believe it is very important that we take a careful look in committee at the arrangements set out in the legislation creating an arm's length relationship between the museums and the Government.
It is crucial that these arrangements give the museums the intended autonomy.
These four autonomous museums along with the sub-museums provided for in the legislation are an important part of Canada's identity. They are showcases of our history, our achievement, our art and our future. As Hon. Members know, this country is rich in history. We have an exciting history and everyone should appreciate it.
From the Canadian art displayed in the National Gallery to the Imax/Omnimax theatre in the new Museum of Civilization, these museums reflect the Canadian people. This is invaluable to our country.
It is notable that the legislation specifically mentions for the first time sub-museums such as the Museum of Contemporary Photography and the Canadian War Museum. This will ensure that these museums are not integrated into the larger museums and that they maintain a certain degree of autonomy. I am certain that this will be reassuring to the many supporters of the War Museum. I can only hope that the Government will follow this up with increased funding for this important part of Canadian heritage.
The War Museum is especially important as it is a means of preserving our heritage. I want to share in the remarks of my hon. colleague from Hamilton-Wentworth who so correctly pointed out that this is not a celebration of war but a commemoration and remembrance of the great men and women who have fallen in upholding the security of Canada. Of course, the War Museum is a way of honouring those Canadians who served Canada during the two world wars and a way of preserving Canada's military history.
Many of my constituents are concerned about this. They want to be certain that the War Museum does not lose out to the Museum of Civilization. It would be a great loss if this were to happen. It would also be a great loss if we did not expand the facilities of the War Museum. Valuable war art and other artifacts belonging to the War Museum are in storage as there is not enough display space available. These items should be on display. As one of my colleagues pointed out, we are talking about art worth $500 million. These items should be on display in the National Capital Region and in regimental museums across this great land.
It is also notable that the legislation includes regional outreach in the mandates of the four museums. This allows Canadians living outside the National Capital Region to share in this important national resource. It is
May 25, 1989

essential that Canadians be able to appreciate Canadian art and culture regardless of whether they live in Fredericton, Vancouver or Flin-Flon, Manitoba.
My hon. friend from Burnaby-Coquitlam pointed out some concerns about employees of the museums. These are questions that should be dealt with in committee and I would hope that we could deal with those adequately when the committee studies this Bill.
In conclusion, I want to say again how pleased I am to see the progress that has been made by Canada's national museums. There are now four independent museums, and in my opinion, that is a step forward. All Canadians benefit from the growth in these institutions and we are all proud to see them develop into world class showcases for Canadian science, art and civilization.
One of my friends in the New Democratic Party raised the issue of appointments to the four separate boards, appointments that will be made by the Hon. Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse). I hope that when appointments are made in the future, they are made on the basis of competence and ability and not on a political basis. It was correctly pointed out that there have been appointments made in the past that can be characterized as political. In fact, politics was the only reason for these appointments. He said: Madam Speaker, I am pleased this afternoon to present Bill C-206, an Act to change the boundaries of the National Capital Region, to the House. This Bill is a suggestion and I must give all due credit to the Mayor of Rockland, His Worship Jean-Marc Lalonde, who in 1986 had this brilliant idea to extend the boundaries of the National Capital Region. His Worship later contacted me and asked me whether it would be possible to take similar action. What I did, Madam Speaker, is first to contact the National Capital Commission to have its reaction to this proposal.

On June 27, 1988, at the Government Operations Committee, the Chairman of the National Capital Commission in response to a question that I asked said the following:
It would be wonderful if perhaps you had a Private Member's bill in which you would suggest the boundaries of the National Capital Region be extended, especially along the Ottawa River. That would, I think, delight our hearts because we feel that the protection of the banks of the Ottawa River is just perhaps one of the most important issues that we face.
That is the position that was expressed to the parliamentary committee at that time concerning this particular Private Member's Bill.
Following this statement by the Chairman of the National Capital Commission, I had a meeting in the fall of 1988 with the municipalities potentially involved in such a venture. At the meeting that was held at the Township of Clarence town hall were present representatives of the eight municipalities potentially affected. Those municipalities would be the Township of Clarence, the Town of Rockland, the Township of Cambridge, the Village of Casselman, the Township of North Planta-

May 25, 1989
National Capital Act
genet and South Plantagenet and the Village of Planta-genet itself.
What does the Private Member's Bill do, and what is the cost to the taxpayers of Canada? The Private Member's Bill would add eight municipalities to the some 50 or so municipalities that already form part of the National Capital Region. What would this cost the taxpayers of Canada? The short answer is nothing. Extending the boundaries of the National Capital Region does not in itself cause any cost other than the cost of redoing the map of the National Capital Region and printing the Private Member's Bill in question into the statute upon its promulgation.
What are some of the benefits to us? There are some benefits in both the short and the long term. In the short term, the obvious benefit to the constituents that I represent would surely be in the fact that the National Capital Region would then designate their municipalities. In other words, if one is an industrialist arriving at the Ottawa International Airport and picking up a regular tourist map of the National Capital Region, communities such as Rockland, Plantagenet, Casselman and so on that are very close to the National Capital Region and very close to Parliament Hill would then form part of the map in question. It would demonstrate that indeed these communities are near the National Capital area.
There would be a benefit to tourism for the constituents that I represent. All of this, I suggest again, would be at very little if any cost to the taxpayers. One might ask, if such is the case, why does it cost us so much to have the NCC now? The short answer to that is very simply that in one municipality of my riding, the Township of Russell, the National Capital Commission has never spent one cent in that particular municipality. I am informed by my colleague from Gatineau-La Lievre (Mr. Assad) that the same is true for a number of municipalities which he represents so ably in the House of Commons.
Therefore, the National Capital Commission does not spend money in all the municipalities which are within its territory. Of course we would wish that eventually the NCC would provide assistance of one sort or another to the municipalities in question. But the Bill in itself by its
adoption does not automatically result in any expenditure of any kind in that regard.
What are some of the benefits? I have already spoken about the fact that there are potential tourism benefits for the area. What is the benefit for this country as a whole, some Members across the way might ask? Quite simply, it is the following: We have recognized as a Parliament in the past that it was necessary to have a National Capital Act. We have felt that it was desirable to have such an Act in order to protect an area around the National Capital Region. Therefore, the need to have such an Act has been well established and historically recognized by the Parliament of this country. Why should it be extended eastward, and what benefit would all of Canada derive from that?
One of the most precious and historical rivers in this country on which one of the founders of this country, Samuel de Champlain, sailed in the 1600s, is indeed the Ottawa River, and it goes through the constituency that I represent. It is a very historic river. There a few islands on the river. Those islands are important from a conservation standpoint. The banks of the Ottawa River should indeed be protected and preserved. Right now there is nothing to preserve the banks of the Ottawa River in that area. There is nothing to protect the islands and to keep them in the public domain for future generations to enjoy. I would suggest that these islands warrant protection. This has been recognized by a statement made by Mrs. Jean Pigott on June 27, 1988 which I recited to your Honour in the House of Commons a few moments ago.
There is one further point which I think should be brought to the attention of this House. It is the following: If one were to leave Parliament Hill right now and drive in a westerly direction to the limit of the National Capital Region, one would find that the distance from Parliament Hill to the westerly limit of the National Capital Region is some 45 kilometres. If one goes eastward from Parliament Hill to the easterly limit of the National Capital Region, one would find that that distance is only 20 to 25 kilometres. What I am proposing in this Bill, and what has been suggested and brought to our attention here by His Worship, the Mayor of Rockland, Mr. Jean-Marc Lalonde, is that we extend the boundary eastward to a distance which is similar to what the distance is on the western side of the city.
May 25, 1989



In other words, what we want to do with this Bill is quite simply to extend the territory of the National Capital, not very far, just as far east of Ottawa as the Region extends west of Ottawa.

Just in case some may think that this initiative is not one that enjoys the support of the local municipalities I have in hand here, and I have provided a copy of the same documentation to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. MacKay) and to other Members of this House, particularly the Member for the New Democratic Party, whom I understand is interested in speaking on this issue, a copy of all the resolutions of the municipal councils in question adopting this initiative.

Mr. Speaker, this initiative has the unanimous support of the eight municipalities concerned. I have in my hand a resolution passed by the Council of Clarence Township; I have a resolution from the Town of Rockland; I have here a resolution from the municipalities of Plantagenet South and Plantagenet North, from the Village of Casselman, from the Municipality of Cambridge and the Village of Plantagenet. So it is clear that all the municipalities concerned are unanimously in favour of this initiative.
I would also like to bring to the attention of the House a report published in May 1988 for the Council of the United Counties of Prescott and Russell by the consulting firm of Leroux & Associates who recommended that the region I just described to the House be annexed to the territory of the National Capital. This report is called "One Step from the National Capital Region."
Mr. Speaker, in closing, I would like to point out some other important facts. I could describe the region I represent and I could for quite a while longer tell the House all the good reasons for passing this Bill.
However, it is important in the House today that we do not create a circumstance which may cause certain MPs to be tempted to talk this Bill out. For the information of all who are listening, and for the information of all who will read Hansard in the future and who may not be familiar with the procedure of the House, there is a
National Capital Act
quick and easy way for the Government to ensure that the Bill is defeated without voting against it, and that way is to talk it out. In other words, ensure that a government Member is standing on his feet at six o'clock. That has been done in the past by certain Hon. Members, and by some political Parties that do not wish to vote against a legislative measure of one form or another.
I want to suggest to the House that this not be done, that we allow this item to come to a vote today and we dispose of the item in question, hopefully disposing of it in favour.
A project of a similar nature involving the Blue Water Bridge proposed by the Conservative Member for that region last year was voted on on the same day by all Members of the House. We talked briefly on the Bill in question and all Members co-operated in ensuring that the Bill was not talked out.
What I am asking for today is exactly the same courtesy that was offered at that time to an issue that was not partisan, but which benefited local municipalities in one Member's riding. As I understand that particular venture, it involved very little cost to the taxpayers.
This Bill has many similarities to the one passed in the House of Commons approximately one year ago involving the Blue Water Bridge. I hope and trust that all Hon. Members will allow this issue to come to a vote in order that the Mayor of Rockland and the mayors of all other municipalities, and the Council of the United Counties of Prescott-Russell, can benefit from this measure that we can give to them as a Parliament.
It is often said that the federal Government is very distant to local communities, and that the things we do are not always tangible or there for local people to understand, and that because of the size and the vastness of this country the federal Government is aloof to the every-day needs of Canadians. We have the opportunity now to prove that we can think of the small municipality, that we can help the man on the street, and we can help the constituency which I represent. I urge all my colleagues in the House to support this measure.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few comments about this Bill. I understand the comments of the Hon. Member, and I also appreciate that this is not necessarily a partisan matter. However, it is a matter that should be viewed from the point of view of other parts of the country and

how they might see this if we were to do something like this here today.
I would like to respond to the call from the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Bou-dria) for the enlargement of the National Capital Region to include nearly 400 additional square miles of his riding.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL CAPITAL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Four hundred square miles?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   NATIONAL CAPITAL ACT MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
How many miles do you believe it is? It is nearly 400.
We must look at this Bill and ask ourselves the question, what do we want Ottawa to be as the nation's capital, and then weigh the costs and benefits.
The National Capital Commission, the Crown corporation which administers this new area, sees our capital as Canada's meeting place, as a tool for communicating Canada to Canadians and to the world, and as a place for safeguarding Canada's treasures.
What is a capital for Canadians? What do we hope for when we go to Ottawa or see it on television? What will foreign guests learn about us when visiting Ottawa?
We want something to be proud of. Ottawa should be a place that everyone in the country would call their own, a capital where the Government listens to their voices and lets them realize their dreams wherever they might live. That is what we want to show the world, not some ornamental seat of empire, but the hub of real democracy.
That means that the town should be kept respectable. Frankly, when Ottawa became the capital, it was a mosquito-ridden, swampy logging town that would not justify being the capital of a nation such as ours. However, Canadians who now visit Ottawa know that that is not the case. Over the years, Ottawa has become a comfortable, clean and beautiful capital, worth a visit if you can afford to get here.
The National Capital Commission has had a lot to do with that. National leaders such as John Diefenbaker have seen to the transformation of this city through the NCC. People such as the Hon. Member for Glengarry-
Prescott-Russell have arranged to commemorate our former national leaders near Parliament Hill.
However, people from my riding would probably be surprised to know about some of the other changes around Ottawa. The NCC has had its share of criticism. Some people, for example the Nielsen task force on program review, voiced concerns that the House needs to consider when we talk about Bill C-206.
When I went to school in the Town of Bruce, Alberta, we were taught that Queen Victoria made the City of Ottawa the capital of this country back in the 1850s. It was not Hull, which is the major town across the Ottawa River, certainly not the Town of Amprior, Ontario, or the Township of Buckingham, Quebec.
In 1969 the federal and provincial Governments agreed that the National Capital Region would include all those places, and all those places would have the benefit of the National Capital Commission. In all, 26 municipalities in Ontario and Quebec are now part of the region. Some of these have effectively become part of Ottawa, for example, Nepean. Others, like Amprior, are quite separate towns or villages. They are not Ottawa and do not look like Ottawa. All of the areas that Bill C-206 would add to the NCC is like that: very nice places, but not the nation's capital.
The federal lands, green parklands and buildings that the NCC owns are now four times the size of the whole City of Ottawa. The NCC is the capital's biggest land owner.
This federal agency is no municipal Government. It does not collect garbage or run buses. No local officials sit on its Board of Commissioners. However, its budget is nearly half the size of the budget of the City of Ottawa. It was $92,261,000 in the Main Estimates for 1988-89.
The NCC employs more than 900 people. It sponsors cultural events and festivals. It plants more than 500,000 tulips in five hectares of flower beds. It manages 300 kilometres of pathways, 668 hectares of parks, 2,230 hectares of turf, and many museums and other buildings.
No wonder this Commission costs so much money. No wonder towns such as Rockland, Plantagenet, St. Isidore de Prescott and others would like in on the action.
