There are probably towns just across Ottawa on the other side of the river that would like to become part of the National Capital Region. The Member has been quite vocal on the subject of this expansion. He and his supporters say that the NCC would maintain riverside parks further down the Ottawa River, along the South Nation River, and prevent erosion.
NCC pamphlets would include these new towns for business and tourism promotion. Perhaps new federal buildings would go up in these towns and attack unemployment and a poor tax base in this mostly rural riding.
These are normal and understandable concerns in a riding with a weaker economy. The Hon. Member's constituents have watched this care and attention going on next door, and they feel it would be beneficial to have those types of improvements in their area as well.
Where I disagree with this Bill is that it seeks to do these things at federal expense at a time when we have just had to make over $5 billion in spending cuts just to keep our heads above water. When we cannot pay for 14 military bases, we cannot pay for more tulips.
As the Nielsen task force report said about the NCC: "Ownership begets more ownership which results in ever-increasing development and operating expenses". Is that not what this Bill is really about?
What we have heard so far has little to do with the way the NCC sees this town of Ottawa, or the way many Canadians see the capital. How many Canadians know the area around Ottawa? How many, if asked, would say that the area makes them feel part of the business of the country?
Back in Roman times there were two kinds of laws. The first kind were leges. These were laws to benefit Rome and its citizens as a whole. The other kind were privi-leges, which is where the word "privilege" comes from. These laws were only for a few people, giving them special rights. I think Bill C-206 is just that, a privilege and probably not much more.

We could expand the NCC forever, north, south, east and west, and there would always be someone left out, like the West Edmonton Mall. I cannot support this Bill or its progress through the House for that reason.
I do not want to suggest in any way that I am saying anything negative about the people of his riding or the people who live in those towns and communities. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, first I want to salute my colleague. It is a laudable idea and I applaud him for his initiative. If I were in his constituency, I would probably do the very same thing and would be remiss and perhaps criticized if I did not.
Much work has gone into this Bill, and various municipalities are involved. I know full well the frustrations of a municipal politician, having spent 10 years in that particular line of work. I know that they are behind the project.
The benefits are obvious. Ottawa and area is a beautiful place to visit. It is a showcase for Canada. It is a pleasure to be here. In fact, it is the second most favourable city I would like to be in, second only to Sault Ste. Marie.
Canadians must be proud to visit their capital and the NCC has done very much to make this more than a liveable city and area, with an exemplary life-style. Other Canadian cities may in fact be jealous of the moneys spent, but their nationalism shines through and they say it is probably money well spent.
Having said this, I must add some criticism, not of the project or the concept or the initiative, but to some of the changes in direction and philosophy of the NCC. I have read the NCC corporate plan and have some grave concerns about the terminology used and some of its probable consequence.

National Capital Act
As I read through the corporate plan I see phrases like market approach, market driven, revenue generation ventures, user fees, contracting out. This sounds very much like another agenda that we have become used to in this recent Thirty-fourth Parliament. I have great fears that the two agendas will come together, and I do not believe that is something we want to endorse, because the endorsation of that particular corporate plan would be an endorsation of the Government's plan.
We have concerns about the apparent change and the less than subtle approach of the NCC to doing business.
The NCC should definitely be at arm's length from the Government, and we have grave concerns that that arm is being amputated at bit at a time, if there is such a possibility.
One has to wonder about the timing of this initiative, however laudable, when there is a reduction in funding of $5 million. We are not yet sure how that will be addressed. As recently as yesterday afternoon, Mrs. Pigott could not say how the $5 million reduction would be addressed.
The request is for an expansion of territory only to be coincident with a reduction in funding. My hon. colleague suggests that this will cost nothing. I accept that it will probably cost nothing now, but certainly one has to be realistic and suggest that it will cost something in the distant future.
This concept of expansion yet reduction is tantamount to spending $27,000 on a shrub inventory, $48,000 on a poll to find out what Canadians think of the NCC, and spending $1.6 million on studies at at time when the Government says we must cut back. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has said that the shrub inventory expenditure is stupid spending, but we all know it is business as usual. The inventory went ahead.
We all know that studies beget studies, to parahrase what was in the corporate plan. Studies are often put on the shelf where they gather dust. If they are not acted on with some immediacy, a new study will eventually be required when it is necessary to rationalize spending five years later. We cannot tighten our belts, pull in, and let out our trousers at the same time. Something will give. I
will not pursue that analogy, but one can see the consequences of trying to do this.
We support the concept of decentralization. Our Party supports that principle strongly. I hope a federal building is erected in Plantagenet, Casselman and Prescott-

The point of this document is that it is a sound bit of work by municipal authorities who are very interested in seeing the benefits that come from being within the National Capital Region extended to their area. In my review of it I see that there are at least five major characteristics of Prescott-Russell which the report suggests make it suitable to be part of the National Capital Region.
The first relates to demographic position and emphasizes the largely Francophone population in the area in question. However, I feel that given that about half the National Capital Region already in existence is in part of the Province of Quebec and has a large majority of Francophone population that it is not clear from the report that there would be any significant difference on this importance balance within the National Capital Region. I think we want to do more than just play with some numbers and statistics here. The fact is that the National Capital Region is most certainly a present reflection of the duality of Canada and our two founding cultures. The suggestion in the report that this would be altered by the inclusion of this more eastern part, while it is an important point, I do not think can really be considered to be fundamentally significant in a way that would influence us here.
National Capital Act
The report goes on to deal with the Ottawa River shoreline, tourist circuits and attractions, festivals and organizations. Those are the five main characteristics cited in it in support of the contention that the boundary be drawn to a more easterly point. Again, one cannot take exception with any of those points. For example, in terms of festivals, the national capital now has the reputation of being an active and dynamic city in a wide range of festivals and special events that occur throughout the year. It is a real treat for Canadians from any part of the country, and foreigners as well, to come to the National Capital Region to participate in these seasonal festivals.
The argument that was put forward in the Prescott- Russell report to which I have already made reference is that the inclusion of Prescott-Russell would provide additional partners to be involved in festivals and special events. At the present time the NCC, which hosts several major festivals in the capital, has an extensive network of partners both in the public and private sectors. There are a number of other agencies as well that sponsor festivals with a local audience and a local character. It is questionable that the addition of even more partners would have a significant positive impact. In fact, it is quite possible that the opposite result would be achieved in terms of overburdening the existing administrative structure.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the debate on Bill C-206, an Act to change the boundaries of the National Capital Region. I understand very well why our colleague, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Bou-dria), introduced this Private Member's Bill. I understand his interest. I know that for a Member of Parliament, it is politically very profitable, but I believe that the present boundaries of the National Capital Region are reasonable and acceptable.
The most important feature of Private Members' Bills, of course, is that Hon. Members of all parties have the opportunity to analyse them together, as well as the chance to develop and put forward new legislation. And as individuals, we are all free to vote for or against these Bills, whatever side of the House we are on.
I must express serious reservations about the justification of Bill C-206, which seeks to extend or enlarge the National Capital Region.
The principle underlying this expansionist idea is outdated these days, when we must constantly strive to do more with less. Furthermore, Madam Speaker, the hypothesis that the municipalities concerned will all enjoy a whole range of benefits paid for by the federal Government is to my mind doubtful and unverified.
What are our priorities as a government during this period of restraint and restructuring? I believe that most Canadians agree that we must adopt less expansionary, less costly policies-not the other way around. I also believe that Canadians in general are in favour of more regionally based government and development, as the previous speaker said.
National Capital Act
Needless to say, the National Capital Region is a special case because the federal Government is located there. It is the only region in the country in which all Canadians have common interests. That is why the federal Government has a special interest in protecting the symbolism it reflects.
The National Capital Region has roughly the shape of a square, the cities of Ottawa and Hull being located near the centre, towards the east. We have Gatineau Park and the Lievre River valley on the Quebec side and the Mississipi and Rideau River valleys on the Ontario side.
The Bill before the House today would add about 400 square miles of Ontario territory adjacent to the eastern boundary of the region. The result would be rather disconcerting. If our calculations are correct, this protuberance would increase the region's area by 22 per cent.
We must not forget another important point, which is that the Capital National Region has 40 per cent more territory in Ontario than in Quebec. The Bill would merely increase the present imbalance.
I am not trying to draw nice straight boundary lines on a map. The issue goes much further. The National Capital Region is a symbol, uniting as it does the two main cultural and linguistic groups in this country. It is a living expression of the link between those groups, which should be represented fairly and equitably. This Bill tends to undermine this objective.
In concluding, Madam Speaker, I would like to point out that there is also the tourism aspect. As you know, many Canadians come to visit our Capital, and they come from all electoral districts of our country. They come with their families, in small groups or on organized tours. As Members, we have the privilege of receiving these people. Many tourists come to admire our treasures and national monuments and to learn something about their government and their Canadian cultural heritage. In many cases, they come to take part in our national holidays, while many only stay in the region for a few days. In fact, relatively few visitors go beyond Ottawa's metropolitan area, unless they are staying with relatives or friends who live in rural or semi-rural areas or are visiting Gatineau Park or the nature areas in the Green Belt.
Why expand the National Capital Region, Madam Speaker? Some people would rather make it smaller, although I don't support the idea. I do realize that supporters of this position have some valid arguments. First of all, the Government is divesting itself of goods and responsibilities that are more appropriately the purview of other levels of government or the private

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the adjoumement debate this evening.
Madam Speaker, I am sure you will recall that in this House on April 19, 1989 I asked a question to the Minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation. I asked the Minister why he was planning to attend a conference to be held by the Fraser Institute, a far right organization intent on privatizing first-class mail delivery.
The Minister responsible for the Canada Post Corporation responded, and I quote:
I realize that a closed mind is more appealing to Members of the Liberal Party, but I think that to fulfil one's responsibilities, one should be open to new ideas. The fact that things worked last century does not mean that they have to be strictly adhered to this century.
So, Madam Speaker, the position of the Conservative Government with respect to Canada Post first-class mail is that it is in fact an antiquated system which must be abolished.
However I can tell you, Madam Speaker, that wanting to keep first-class mail in the public sector in Canada is not an antiquated principle.

The Fraser Institute is sponsoring this seminar to be held on January 23 at the Royal York Hotel in Toronto. The seminar's keynote speakers are none other than Don Lander, the President of Canada Post and the Minister responsible for the Post Office.
Canada's universal mail service, which has served to unify this country, has been in place since the existence of Canada, and it was even in place after the Act of Union of 1840 which linked the colonies of Upper and Lower Canada. The rationale for Government-sponsored universal mail service was that the lucrative routes in large cities and linking large cities where the profits are would be made to subsidize mail service to small and remote communities across the country.
It is well known by the Canadian public that Canada Post does not make money when people send money orders from Trois Pistoles to Wetaskiwin or from St. Isadore de Prescott to a community east of Montreal. That is not where the money is at Canada Post.
Indeed, some 50 per cent of Canada's revenue, or close to it, is generated by first-class mail. Therefore, the first-class mail service is what subsidizes and keeps the rest of the system going.
What is happening now? The Minister responsible for Canada Post and the Corporation has privatized rural mail service. The Government has reduced services in urban areas, replacing door-to-door service with so-called supermailboxes which no one likes.
Postal outlets are replacing full post offices that once existed in rural communities. On top of that, the Government is now saying that it has an open mind about attending a conference which aims to privatize first-class mail, the mail which keeps everything else going.
I submit that if in fact first-class mail is privatized, we will destroy the postal system altogether for it is the revenue from first-class mail that keeps the postal system going. I urge the Government to make forthwith, through the spokesperson designated today, assurances that first-class mail will not be privatized. No country in
May 25, 1989

the western world has done so, not even the country of that great proponent of privatization, Margaret Thatcher. Even Mrs. Thatcher, notwithstanding her views on privatization, has not attempted to do anything like privatize first-class mail. She knows better. I am asking now, does the Government across know better?

Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Bou-dria) would like to have everyone believe that this Government is about to make fundamental changes to the structure and mandate of Canada Post Corporation and that in fact these changes would leave Canadians with a poor and unreliable postal system.
Let me take this opportunity to assure the Hon. Member that the Government has no present intention of fundamentally changing the structure or mandate of Canada Post Corporation. The Minister responsible for the Post Office said in a recent interview that he was not working on a proposal to get rid of the monopoly that the corporation has on first-class letter mail. Let me also say that this Government has always been willing to listen to the views of Canadians. It is the people of Canada who keep raising the question of the corporation's exclusive mandate. As the Minister said, people are suggesting it, and it would be foolish not to examine it.
The Post Office is not a static institution, one that is entrenched in old ways of doing things. It is an institution that is constantly evolving and changing just like the country and the people for whom it exists to serve. Together let us look at some of those changes. Twenty years ago, the Post Office operated in a very sheltered environment. Today, it is facing competition on all fronts. The corporation is meeting that competition head on by providing Canadians with an efficient, reliable and affordable postal service.
In 1981, all three political parties agreed that the Post Office should become a Crown corporation. At that time, its annual deficit was running at $600 million and increasing annually. This year, Canada Post Corporation will be recording a profit. This means that for the first time in years, Canadians will not pay twice for their
Adjournment Debate
postal service: once when they purchase their stamps, and a second time when they pay their taxes.
Canada Post Corporation is aware that its existence is dependent on the quality of its service. The quality of that service has been getting better. Canada Post Corporation is the only postal system in the world whose delivery performance is measured by independent auditors. The audits which are issued quarterly have clearly shown that significant improvements have occurred in the reliability of on-time mail delivery. For example, in the quarterly performance report issued by Clarkson Gordon, it was reported that 94 per cent of all properly prepared first-class mail within the same province reached its delivery target, and 96 per cent between provinces. Those are some very impressive improvements, and they have been made throughout Canada Post. What is equally impressive is that the corporation is trying, and I believe succeeding, to do even better.

REVENUE CANADA-SPECIAL AUDIT OF AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT TRADE-IN ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to pursue further a question which I directed to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Jelinek) on April 25 of this year concerning what is euphemistically known as the business investment tax credit, heavy equipment trade-in over allowance special audit. That sounds complicated and it is. It is a problem that arises out of the Business Investment Ihx Credit Program which was instituted in 1976. It provided a credit within the Province of Saskatchewan of 10 per cent of the purchase price of a new piece of farm machinery or equipment to be applied against a farmer's federal income tax payable.
That credit acted as a considerable stimulus for machinery transactions and was, needless to say, well received in the farm community. In fact, some farmers built up such a credit that I believe in 1983 the then Government of the day instituted a further refinement of the program to permit a cash rebate to the farmer of 40 per cent of the unused credits. That in turn exacerbated the problem which I will enlarge upon.
The difficulty lay in the design of the program. The program was intended, as it turned out, not to stimulate the construction or the manufacture of farm machinery and equipment, but rather to try to stimulate employment on the western prairies with the theory that a farmer having spent $150,000 on a new four-wheel

May 25, 1989
Adjournment Debate
tractor would go to the labour pool and hire some stranger to ride it around in the field for him. That is a sad example of the type of twenty-third floor, ivory-tower, bureaucratic thinking in this place.
Regardless of the intent behind that ill-conceived Liberal program, and which our Government to its credit has phased out through 1986, 1987, and 1988, we have to face the problem that farmers of course took advantage of the program in the trading in of their machinery and equipment. What happened was that farm machinery manufacturers and dealers got into the habit of inflating the value of farm machinery and equipment that was traded in. A brand new tractor might carry the price of $100,000.
If a farmer was trading in a piece of equipment that was worth $10,000, $90,000 cash would be paid as the difference. However, it was also open to the dealer to raise the list price of that tractor to $150,000 and inflate the value of the farmer's trade-in from $10,000 up to $60,000. The farmer did not care. In fact, in many cases the farmer did not know, because he was still paying the same amount of cash difference. The fact is that as far as the treasury of the country is concerned, the rebate of 10 per cent on the new price which ordinarily would have been 10 per cent of $100,000 in fact became 10 per cent of $150,000. We are talking about sizeable amounts of money. Over the course of the program, I would estimate that hundreds of millions of dollars were paid out of the federal treasury through this tax expenditure program which in essence was a mini-scientific research tax credit plan. The moneys would have been better spent, as they are now, targeted toward universal programs for Canadian farmers.
In any event, the problem is that along the way Revenue Canada decided that it would attack the western Canadian farmer and state that he was abusing the program by artificially inflating the value of those pieces of machinery and equipment that were traded in.
The producer in western Canada is the innocent party in all of this. If there was abuse of the program, first we must say that the program was ill-conceived, ill-designed, and tailor-made for problems to develop. That is
problem number one. It was the policy of the then Government that was clearly at fault. Second, it was the manufacturers of equipment and the dealer networks which I believe really got into the game of inflating trade-in values.
The average farmer is no different from a person living in the city. If they have a vehicle that they want to trade in, they are going to shop around from dealer to dealer and say: "I would like to buy a new whatever. I have this vehicle to trade in. How much cash difference do I have to pay?" That is the only concern that a particular farmer would have with regard to this matter.
Now we have the spectacle of Revenue Canada coming along years after the fact saying to a farmer: "Well, we think that we are going to reassess you because you abused this program. You arbitrarily increased the value of the piece of equipment that you traded in and we are going to reassess you, cut down that value, and come after you with the full force of the law". If Revenue Canada were allowed to proceed with this folly, it would have entrapped and ensnared virtually every single producer and farmer in western Canada. To the credit of the previous Minister of National Revenue, when he got wind of that proposal on the part of Revenue Canada, he did put a stop to that special audit. However, there were approximately 600 cases where the Department of National Revenue stated that it thought there was abuse and that it should proceed against those farmers.
It is my opinion and the opinion of many farm groups and producer groups in western Canada that that is very unfair. Again, the previous Minister stated that there would be a test case. The crux of the issue here is whether Revenue Canada can come along and substitute its idea of a fair market value of a piece of equipment or machinery that is traded in with its idea of fair market value in place of that freely arrived at in the marketplace between a willing vendor and a willing purchaser acting at arm's length. That really is the legal question involved. I suggest that it is not for Revenue Canada to interfere with that kind of decision. However, Revenue Canada says it can. The previous Minister said there would be a test case to try and decide this matter. Unfortunately, the test case fell apart.
May 25, 1989

I asked the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Jeli-nek) on April 25, 1989, what his intentions were. He indicated at that time that he was working with the community, looking for a new case to come forward and so on. That is fine, and I very much appreciate that response.
What concerned me and caused me to put this item on for debate here was a response from Revenue Canada taxation in Regina on April 26, 1989, the day after the Minister's response. They say they intend to proceed as expeditiously as possible against the taxpayer because this particular test case was not going ahead.
I believe in this situation that the Department is simply out of control. Given the background, the circumstances, the years this program has gone on and the time these people have waited, to proceed originally I believe was fundamentally unfair, and to carry on now I believe is unfair. I would ask the Minister to either find another test case with a suitable agreed statement of facts, or simply drop the entire matter. Justice delayed is no justice.
In conclusion, I am heartened by the presence of the Minister here today to answer to this matter. His very presence leads me to think that he will be taking the matter in hand.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this indeed is a very important issue and that is why I am here personally to respond to a very good case brought forward by my colleague, the Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia (Mr. Wilson).
At the outset, let me say that it is my intent and always has been as Minister of National Revenue to continue to consult, communicate and listen to any taxpayer's concerns and representations. I certainly intend to do so in this instance. If the Hon. Member or any taxpayers or organizations associated with this situation want to meet with me in order for me to hear their side of the story, as has been very well represented by the Hon. Member in the House today and on previous occasions, I would be very happy to meet with them in order to get both sides of the story.
Adjournment Debate
Allow me to put this issue into some perspective. Some time ago the Department undertook to review and audit the income tax returns of certain taxpayers who have claimed investment tax credits on purchases of heavy machinery and equipment. It has been pointed out on numerous occasions that the specific audit program was not restricted to farmers of western Canada, which I want to make clear, but included other industrial sectors, such as logging, transportation, manufacturing and fishing, encompassing all regions of Canada.
The special program phase of this audit activity was concluded in April, 1987, when it reached its goal of identifying those taxpayers who claimed excessive investment tax credit as a result of receiving substantial trade-in allowances on used equipment.
For the time being, the Department will continue to proceed through the normal routine audit program to address significant cases of trading over-allowances. But it has always been the position of the Department that the investment tax credit claim must be based on the actual cost of the property acquired and computed in a manner consistent with the economic reality of that transaction. This position is supported by case law and accounting principles, and is set out in a 1987 information circular which reiterated the long-standing positions of the Department as set out in previous bulletins.
However, to remove any uncertainty as to the Department's determination of capital cost in these circumstances, and in fairness to the taxpayer, the Department was prepared to have the matter settled by the courts if the taxpayers were to challenge the Department's interpretation of the Act. Such a case was brought forward but was withdrawn by the taxpayer who decided to accept the Department's position.
It is my hope that another representative test case will emerge in order that this matter can be resolved fairly and equitably by the courts, hopefully to everyone's satisfaction. I urge the Member and the affected community and individuals to do just that. We do not have control of the test case. We want the community to come forward with the test case so that the taxpayer can be treated fairly and honourably. speakerposition: N.D.P. Deputy House Leader
subtopic: REVENUE CANADA-SPECIAL AUDIT OF AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT TRADE-IN ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to express dissatisfaction with the answer given to me in the House on April 5 of this year by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) in regard to VIA Rail. The date is important since it is prior to the now infamous Budget which veiy clearly was designed to lead to the inevitable destruction of VIA Rail as the provider of passenger rail service in Canada.
I would like first to refer to the question that I put to the Minister and the answer that I received. I told the Minister of Transport:
When the Liberals tried to cut the deficit by taking apart VIA Rail, just like this Government appears to be set on doing, the now Deputy Prime Minister took a PC Task Force across this country in defence of VIA Rail. Its report entitled "The Last Straw" concluded that the federal Government has a responsibility to ensure that rail passenger services in Canada be retained, modernized, and expanded as an important part of our national transportation system.
If my memory serves me correctly the Conservative Party ran on that as part of its platform plank in 1984.1 will give the Party credit for this, immediately after it was elected it did reinstate services which had been cut by the former Liberal Government. However, that is where the situation ends.
I asked the Minister on April 5 if the Government would live up to its report and its promises as stated in 1984 by ensuring that VIA will not only receive the funds necessary to maintain its existing operations but funds to modernize its operations.
The Minister stated:
The answer was that any decision concerning VIA Rail or any other Crown corporation for that matter will be made in due time.
Due time came along fairly soon with the Budget. The Budget indicated that there would be a reduction in the level of subsidy to VIA Rail. In fact, it turns out that that reduction has a value of approximately $1.2 billion over the next five years. Depending on who one talks to that reduction could have a number of results.
The worst case scenario is that because of the ever decreasing dollars available from the federal coffers that it will not be five years from now that VIA as we know it as a national passenger rail system will cease to exist but it might be this fall. I am aware that on June 15 VIA Rail will increase its prices for every passenger, whether that be a day coach passenger, an overnight passenger, or what have you, by 10 per cent. The last time prices were raised by 10 per cent VIA Rail lost in excess of 700,000 passengers. VIA Rail knows this. The Government knows this. I am sure that is part and parcel of the over-all plan for the destruction of VIA Rail.
The Government has said it will protect nine routes where the people who live along those routes have no other alternative in terms of transportation. They are captive to rail. However, when it comes down to that final year, when there will be only $250 million of subsidy available to VIA, many of us believe that all that it will be able to afford to operate will be those nine routes. That means no Atlantic, no Transcontinental and that the run from Jasper to Vancouver will be gone from the national system.
It may mean that the corridor, Windsor, Toronto, Ottawa, Montreal, Quebec City is also gone. In addition, there is the collective agreement reality between VIA Rail and some of its employees. That makes the cost of shutting down the system extremely expensive as a means of protecting the workers, who will sort of feel like they were employees of CN Route, as they have been transferred over from CN to VIA, or CP to VIA, and who now find after a very few years that their jobs are going out the window or have been dropped off at the end of the-I would say caboose, but that is gone too.
This Government has made a conscious decision to eliminate rail passenger services as a national system. It is talking about provincialization. I hope there is no province that says yes.
I wrote to the Premiers right after the budget decision and said: "If you do that then you are falling into the trap once again of allowing the federal Government to offload national programs and put them to the provinces where the provincial taxpayers have to pay the tab."
May 25, 1989

I say to you, Madam Speaker, and to the Government of Canada, VIA Rail is extremely important. It is the only method of travel for hundreds of thousands of Canadians. It is a great tourist opportunity. The Government is wrong in what it is doing. What it is doing is driving the last spike through the heart of VIA Rail. Not only should it be ashamed of itself for doing it, but it should reconsider what it is doing, live up to its own promises to the Canadian people and make sure that VIA Rail continues to exist.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Government House Leader):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
subtopic: REVENUE CANADA-SPECIAL AUDIT OF AGRICULTURAL EQUIPMENT TRADE-IN ALLOWANCES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Government appreciates the concerns of those who have expressed their support for rail passenger services. However, I think it is fair to say that the Government has come to the conclusion that Canadian taxpayers can no longer afford ever-increasing subsidies to rail passenger services.
Since 1984, the Government has contributed $600 million towards capital investment to the modernization of VIA's services. However, the operating subsidies have continued to increase. Over the past four years, total federal subsidies to VIA have increased from $607 million in 1985 to $641 million in 1988.
On May 9,1989, the Government announced that VIA had been asked to prepare and submit by June 30,1989, a new business plan with respect to the new reference
Adjournment Debate
levels for the corporation. These reference levels are, and I would like to read them into the record: $541 million for 1989-90; $435 million for 1990-91; $394 million for 1991-92; $275 million for 1992-93; and $250 million for 1993-94.
The new reference levels reflect the Government's commitment to expenditure reduction and restraint.
The Government expects the corporation to consider all available options in the development of the business plan, including productivity improvements, fare increases, the take-over of services by other interested parties, service reductions and route abandonments.
The Canadian Government's new policy approach for VIA ensures that rail passenger service will be maintained to remote localities which have no other year-round means of transportation. Service will be protected to truly isolated communities along the following remote routes: Jasper to Prince Rupert, The Pas to Lynn Lake, Wabowden to Churchill, Winnipeg to Churchill, Winnipeg to Capreol, Sudbury to White River, Senneterre to Cochrane, Montreal to Senneterre and Montreal to Jonquiere.
